segments.english: The LORD said, "Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,
segments.literal: and-the-LORD said: question-covering I from-Abraham what I doing?

tokens.note: הַ- is the interrogative; the piel participle מְכַסֶּה with it is a question of astonishment (Rashi, בִּתְמִיהָ).

phrases.literal: 'and-the-LORD said'; the Hebrew names no addressee

phrases.english: Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do
phrases.literal: 'question-covering I from-Abraham what I doing'; the question opens the divine speech and is completed in 18:18

grammar: וַיהוָה אָמָר: a vav, then the subject, then a qatal (pausal אָמָר). Because the subject stands before the verb, this is not the plain wayyiqtol of narrative: it is a clause that pauses the story ('now the LORD had said'), or reports a thought (Ramban). The Hebrew gives no addressee.
הַמְכַסֶּה: a piel participle with the interrogative ה, 'am I hiding?'; Rashi reads the ה as a question of astonishment (בִּתְמִיהָ), 'can I hide?'.
אֲשֶׁר אֲנִי עֹשֶׂה is a relative clause with an active participle, which can mean an act in progress or one about to happen; the object is not stated (Rashi supplies 'in Sodom').
The tipḥa on וַיהוָה and the etnaḥta on אָמָר set off the introduction; the mahpakh on הַמְכַסֶּה begins the question, and the silluq closes the verse at עֹשֶׂה.
segments.note: The English keeps the question form. Rashi supplies 'in Sodom' as the object of 'what I am doing'; the English does not add it, and the commentary records it. The quotation is not closed here: the speech runs to the end of 18:19.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the הֲ of הַמְכַסֶּה marks astonishment (בִּתְמִיהָ), so God asks in wonder whether he can hide the matter from Abraham. The English keeps the question.

Rashi: the object is 'in Sodom'. It is not fitting for God to do this without Abraham's knowledge: God gave him this land, and these five cities are his (he cites Gen. 10:19, the border of the Canaanite 'toward Sodom and Gomorrah'); God called him Abraham, father of a multitude of nations, so will he destroy the sons and not tell the father, who loves him? The English 'what I am about to do' does not name Sodom; the supplied object is recorded here.

apparatus: Addressee of the saying: Ramban takes it to be the host of heaven or the messengers, or an inner thought ('every saying with the heart is a thought'); Radak takes it as the God who appeared to Abraham telling him of Sodom in the same vision. The Hebrew names no one.

segments.english: seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed through him?
segments.literal: and-Abraham surely-become shall-become to-a-nation great and-mighty and-shall-be-blessed through-him all nations-of the-earth

tokens.note: The vav gives a reason here (Rashi: 'seeing he is dear to me'); the literal line keeps 'and'.
infinitive absolute before the yiqtol of the same verb: emphasis, 'surely become'.
לְ after a verb of becoming marks the predicate: 'become a nation'.
גָּדוֹל of a nation: great in number and power; sense 2 'great in number' is the one that suits the pairing with עָצוּם ('mighty, numerous').
The lexicon entry lists 'mighty, numerous' with no senses; 'mighty' is the first gloss.
nifal weqatal, third plural, continuing the yiqtol of 18:18.3. The lexicon's 'bless oneself' is the reflexive reading that Ibn Ezra rejects here: the verb is passive.
בְּ with the suffix; Ibn Ezra's בִּשְׁבִילוֹ, 'on his account'.
construct: 'all the nations of'.
the earth as the whole world, not the land of Canaan. The word is ambiguous with 'land' (sense 2).

phrases.english: seeing that Abraham shall surely become
phrases.literal: 'and-Abraham surely-become shall-become'; the vav gives the reason for the question, as in Rashi's plain sense
'to-nation great and-mighty'; the lamed is predicative

phrases.english: and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed through him
phrases.literal: 'and-shall-be-blessed through-him all nations-of the-earth'; the passive follows Ibn Ezra

grammar: הָיוֹ יִהְיֶה: the infinitive absolute before the yiqtol of the same verb intensifies it: 'surely shall become'.
לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל וְעָצוּם: the predicate after הָיָה is marked by the lamed, and the two adjectives are joined by the vav.
וְנִבְרְכוּ בוֹ: the weqatal of the nifal continues the yiqtol of 18:18.3; its subject is 'all the nations', and the verb is passive in Ibn Ezra's reading.
The zaqef qaton on the first word and the tipḥa on גָּדוֹל divide the clause; the silluq closes the verse at הָאָרֶץ.
segments.note: Rashi's midrash is that the name is repeated for a blessing (זֵכֶר צַדִּיק לִבְרָכָה); the plain sense is that God would not hide from one dear to him. The English gives the plain sense. The verse continues the quoted speech begun in 18:17.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the name is given again as a blessing (זֵכֶר צַדִּיק לִבְרָכָה), but the plain sense is 'shall I hide from him, when he is dear to me, to become a great nation and be the blessing of all the nations of the earth'. The English reads the vav as 'since', the reason for the question in 18:17.
Ibn Ezra: the verb is nifal (נפעל), meaning that they will be blessed on his account. The form in 22:18 (והתברכו) is not the same; there they bless themselves. The English is passive.

segments.english: For I have known him, so that he may charge his sons and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD by doing righteousness and justice, in order that the LORD may bring upon Abraham what he spoke concerning him."
segments.literal: for I-have-known-him, in-order-that he-will-charge [object-marker] his-sons and-[object-marker] his-household after-him, and-they-keep the-way-of the-LORD to-do righteousness and-justice, in-order-that the-LORD bring upon-Abraham [object-marker] that he-spoke concerning-him

tokens.note: כִּי: 'for'; it gives the reason why God will not hide his plan (18:17).
יָדַע with a person as object: acquaintance. Rashi reads the word as an expression of affection (חִבָּה), like 'known to her husband' (Ruth 2). Its root sense is knowledge.
לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר + yiqtol: purpose, 'in order that he may ...'. Rashi glosses it 'because' (לְפִי שֶׁ) but allows that it does not suit the Targum's reading; Ramban takes it as purpose.

yiqtol piel after לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר: 'so that he may charge'. The entry gives צָוָה 'lay charge, give charge, command' with no sub-senses. Rashi reads it as a present tense (like Job 1:5), recorded in the commentary.
אֶת before בָּנָיו.
plural of בֵּן; Radak distinguishes the sons from the household (בְּנֵי בֵיתוֹ).
וְאֵת repeats the object marker before the second object.
אַחַר with the suffix: his successors, those who follow him.
weqatal continuing the purpose clause (יְצַוֶּה): 'and they are to keep'; the subject is the sons and the household.
דֶּרֶךְ יְהוָה: the way the LORD requires, in the entry 'way of י׳' (6.e); it is spelled out as 'doing righteousness and justice'.
righteous acts, the object of 'do'.
the second לְמַעַן: purpose, 'in order that'; Rashi reads it so (on 'upon Abraham').
infinitive construct hifil; the English 'may bring' follows the purpose clause.
Rashi: 'upon Abraham', not 'upon his house'.
אֵת before the relative clause.
relative with the marker: 'what he spoke'.
עַל with the suffix: 'concerning him'.

phrases.literal: 'for I-have-known-him'; the word keeps the root 'know' (see context)

phrases.english: to keep the way of the LORD
phrases.literal: 'and-they-keep the-way-of the-LORD'; the weqatal continues the purpose: they are to keep

phrases.english: in order that the LORD may bring

grammar: כִּי יְדַעְתִּיו: qatal, first person singular, with the suffix 'him'; the clause gives the reason why God will not hide the matter. יָדַע with a person as object is 'know a person' (acquaintance, regard, choice).
לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה: לְמַעַן is a preposition of purpose; with אֲשֶׁר it opens a purpose clause and the yiqtol is 'may charge'. The same word opens the second purpose clause (לְמַעַן הָבִיא).
וְשָׁמְרוּ: the weqatal continues the yiqtol of יְצַוֶּה, so the sons and the household are to keep the way of the LORD; לַעֲשׂוֹת states how: by doing righteousness and justice.
הָבִיא is a hifil infinitive construct with לְמַעַן: 'in order that the LORD may bring'.
The revia on יְדַעְתִּיו closes the first clause; the zaqef on אַחֲרָיו and the etnaḥta on וּמִשְׁפָּט mark the later divisions; the silluq closes the verse at עָלָיו.
segments.note: Rashi glosses לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר as 'because' and יְצַוֶּה as a present; but the word is a preposition of purpose and the English reads it so, as Ramban does. The English keeps 'known' for יְדַעְתִּיו, which is Ramban's own choice (knowledge as God's regard for the righteous); Rashi's 'affection' and Ramban's 'I raised him up' are recorded in the commentary. The quotation of the LORD's speech closes here.

commentary.summary: Rashi: ידעתיו is a word of affection (לְשׁוֹן חִבָּה), like מוֹדָע לְאִישָׁהּ (Ruth 2); the root sense of all such words is knowledge, since one who loves draws near and knows the beloved. The English keeps 'known'.

Rashi: לְמַעַן אֲשֶׁר יְצַוֶּה means 'because he commands his sons concerning me to keep my ways'. He adds that if one explains it like the Targum ('I know that he will command ...'), לְמַעַן would not fit the wording. The English declines 'because': it reads לְמַעַן as 'so that', a purpose.
Rashi: יְצַוֶּה is present tense (לְשׁוֹן הוֹוֶה), like 'so Job did' (Job 1:5). The English takes it as the subjunctive of the purpose clause, 'may charge'; his present is recorded here.

Rashi: this is how Abraham commands his sons, 'keep the way of the LORD', in order that the LORD may bring upon Abraham what he spoke. He notes that the verse says 'upon Abraham' and not 'upon the house of Abraham', and draws the homily that whoever leaves a righteous son is as if he had not died. The English reads the second לְמַעַן as purpose; the homily is not the plain sense.

Ramban: he first repeats Rashi (ידעתיו as a word of affection, like 'known to her husband') and adds that if it is explained 'I know that he will command', לְמַעַן does not fit. Another possibility: 'I raised him up so that he would command his sons' (compare Exod. 33:12). He holds that the right sense is knowledge itself: God's knowledge is his providence, which watches the righteous in particular. The English keeps 'known' and reads לְמַעַן as purpose; the 'raised him up' reading is recorded here.

context: The verb 'know' with a person as object can be covenant language: in the treaties of the ancient Near East a great king 'knows' a vassal when he recognizes him as his own partner. Many scholars read 'I have known him' in that sense, 'I have chosen him', and compare Amos 3:2. The medieval commentators differ: Rashi, affection; Ramban, God's attentive regard (and, as a second possibility, 'raised him up').

segments.english: The LORD said to Abraham, "The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has grown great, and their sin is very heavy.
segments.literal: and-said the-LORD outcry-of Sodom and-Gomorrah that-has-grown-great and-their-sin that is-heavy very

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; the speech that opens here runs to the end of 18:21.
construct. Ibn Ezra glosses it as words spoken against God or the outcry of violence (חָמָס); Radak as the cry of the oppressed.
כִּי: 'that', or 'indeed': the outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah, indeed it has grown great; and their sin, indeed it is very heavy.

The parse is a qal qatal, third feminine singular ('has grown great'), but the lemma link in the data goes to the adjective רַב, a different entry; the pack lists no entry for the verb, so no sense is given. Rashi: the accent on the resh marks the verb, 'has grown', not the adjective 'great'.
the second כִּי, parallel to 18:20.6.
Ibn Ezra: so heavy that 'the land cannot hold it' (ולא תכילנה הארץ).

phrases.literal: 'and-said the-LORD'; 'to Abraham' follows Rashi, who has God speak to Abraham

phrases.english: The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah

phrases.literal: 'that has-grown-great'; the accent sets this as 'has grown', per Rashi

grammar: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה: the wayyiqtol introduces the speech, and the Hebrew does not name the one addressed.
זַעֲקַת סְדֹם וַעֲמֹרָה is a construct chain; the outcry is the subject of the first clause.
כִּי רָבָּה: a qatal, third feminine singular, agreeing with זַעֲקָה; the accent above the resh is Rashi's evidence for 'has grown'.
וְחַטָּאתָם כִּי כָבְדָה מְאֹד: a second clause with the same כִּי, so the two clauses stand side by side; the adverb מְאֹד intensifies the qatal.
segments.note: Rashi has the speech addressed to Abraham, and the English says so; Ramban says all the commentators read it that way. The English keeps 'outcry' for זַעֲקַת, which covers both Ibn Ezra's readings; the note records them. The lexicon entry for רבב given in the pack is an adjective; see the note on 18:20.7.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'to Abraham', who had done as God said (not to hide the matter from him). Ramban reports that all the commentators take the speech to Abraham. The English adds 'to Abraham'.

Rashi: every רַבָּה in Scripture has its accent below the bet, because it translates 'great'; this one has it above the resh, because it translates גָּדְלָה, 'has grown'. The English 'has grown great' follows him.
Ibn Ezra: the outcry is either words spoken against God, or the outcry of violence (זעקת החמס). The English keeps 'outcry', and the note records both readings.
Ibn Ezra: 'and their sin, that it is very heavy', so heavy that 'the land cannot bear it' (ולא תכילנה הארץ). The English 'very heavy' gives the sense of כָּבְדָה; his image is recorded in the note.

context: Sodom and Gomorrah are named in the text among the cities of the plain: Gen. 13:12 has Lot settle among them, and Gen. 14:2 names five kings and their cities, Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim and Bela (that is Zoar). The text does not say how many people lived in them.

זְעָקָה is the cry of someone who has been wronged and appeals for redress (compare Gen. 4:10 and Exod. 22:22). In the text's picture of the world such a cry goes up to the deity as judge, who then hears the case.

segments.english: Let me go down now and see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me; and if not, I will find out."
segments.literal: I-will-go-down please and-I-will-see whether-according-to-its-outcry the-coming to-me they-have-done completion, and-if not I-will-know

tokens.note: cohortative. The base text reads אֵֽרְדָה; WLC reads אֵֽרֲדָה (see apparatus).
נָא, a particle of entreaty that softens the cohortative.
the interrogative ה with כְּ. The feminine suffix refers to the city (Sodom): Rashi 'of the city'; Radak takes it as Sodom, mother of the cities.
the article with the qatal is relative: 'that has come'.
Rashi notes a pause (pesiq) between עָשׂוּ and כָּלָה, which separates the two words.

כָּלָה: the noun 'completion, complete destruction' used as an adverb, 'completely, altogether'. Ibn Ezra, at 'ואם לא אדעה': 'I will see whether they all did like this evil'. Rashi and Radak take it as the consequence ('I will make an end of them'); that reading is recorded in the commentary.

Ibn Ezra, the normative commentator: 'I will see whether they all did like this evil'. Rashi: 'I will know what to do' in punishing them with afflictions; recorded in the commentary. Others (in Ibn Ezra): 'I will have mercy' (like 'God knew', Exod. 2:25).

phrases.english: Let me go down now and see
phrases.literal: 'I-will-go-down please and-I-will-see'; two cohortatives, softened by נָא

phrases.english: whether they have done altogether according to the outcry that has come to me
phrases.literal: 'whether-according-to-its-outcry the-coming to-me they-have-done completion'; כָּלָה as an adverbial accusative, 'completely, altogether', Ibn Ezra's 'all of them'; the pesiq after עָשׂוּ makes it a separate word

phrases.english: and if not, I will find out
phrases.literal: 'and-if not I-will-know'; Ibn Ezra: 'I will see whether they all did this evil'

grammar: אֵרְדָה־נָּא וְאֶרְאֶה: two cohortatives, first person singular, 'let me go down' and 'let me see'; נָא softens them.

הַכְּצַעֲקָתָהּ: the interrogative ה, 'whether', with כְּ 'according to' and the noun 'outcry' with the feminine suffix ('its outcry', the outcry of the city; Rashi 'of the city'). הַבָּאָה: the article before the qatal makes a relative clause, 'that has come to me'.

עָשׂוּ כָּלָה: a qatal, third common plural, with כָּלָה. Rashi, Radak and the first view that Ibn Ezra reports take כָּלָה as the consequence ('they will be made an end of'); the pesiq between the words points that way. Ibn Ezra's own view, and Sforno's, take it as 'altogether, all of them'.
וְאִם־לֹא אֵדָעָה: the other half of the alternative, 'and if not, I will know'; the sense is 'see and discern' (Qal 1.c).
segments.note: The English reads one question: God goes down to see whether they have done altogether according to the outcry, and if not, to find out. This is Ibn Ezra's own reading ('I will see whether they all did like this evil'); the apodosis reading ('then I will make an end', Rashi, Radak, and the view he reports first) is recorded. The vowel variant at 18:21.1 does not change the reading.

commentary.summary: Rashi gives two readings of 'I will go down and see': first a homily (the LORD's descent teaches judges to decide capital cases only on evidence); second, 'I will go down to the end of their deeds'. The English keeps 'go down and see'; the second reading is recorded here.
Rashi: הַכְּצַעֲקָתָהּ means 'of the city' (שֶׁל מְדִינָה), the outcry of the city. The English 'the outcry' does not name the city; Rashi's reading is recorded here.

Rashi: if they stand in their rebellion, 'I am making an end of them' (כָּלָה אֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה בָהֶם); if they do not, 'I will know what to do' to punish them with afflictions and not destroy them (compare Exod. 33:5). A pesiq separates עָשׂוּ from כָּלָה. The English does not supply a consequence: it takes כָּלָה as 'altogether', as Ibn Ezra does, and Rashi's reading is recorded here.

Ibn Ezra reports a view ('some say') on הכצעקתה: 'if so, they did, I will make an end of them' (אם כן עשו אעשה בהם כלה), taking כלה as the consequence. His own view is in the next comment ('I will see whether they all did'); the English follows that, not this reading.

Ibn Ezra: of 'and if not, I will know', some explain 'I will have mercy on them' (like 'and God knew', Exod. 2:25); in his own opinion it means 'I will see whether they all did like this evil', since God knows the whole by way of the whole and not by way of a part. (He adds a remark on the pointing of the interrogative ה in הַאַף, 18:23.) The English adopts his view: 'whether they have done altogether ... if not, I will find out'. The mercy reading is recorded here.

apparatus: 18:21.1 vowels: WLC reads אֵֽרֲדָה; the base text reads אֵֽרְדָה. The verb is the same; only the vowels differ.

18:21.7–8 עָשׂוּ ׀ כָּלָה: a pesiq stands between the two words. Rashi, Radak and the first view in Ibn Ezra read 'if they have done according to the outcry, I will make an end (of them)'; Ibn Ezra's own view and Sforno read כָּלָה as 'altogether, all of them'.
context: The LORD 'goes down' to see before judging: in the text's picture of the world he dwells above and comes down to examine a matter on the earth, as in Gen. 11:5. Radak and Rashi take the 'seeing' as teaching men to judge only after looking into a case.

segments.english: The men turned from there and went to Sodom, but Abraham still stood before the LORD.
segments.literal: and-turned from-there the-men and-went Sodom-to and-Abraham still standing before the-LORD

tokens.note: wayyiqtol; 'turned' from the place, i.e. left Abraham's company. Rashi: from the place where Abraham had been escorting them.
מִשָּׁם: adverb with no senses in the lexicon. Rashi: 'from the place where Abraham had been escorting them'.
wayyiqtol; הָלַךְ of persons going (Qal I.1).
directional he with the proper name.
The vav opens a contrast with the departure of the men.
עוֹד with the suffix: 'still'.
participle of a continuing state: he was still standing. Rashi's comment on this word is in the commentary.

phrases.english: but Abraham still stood before the LORD

grammar: וַיִּפְנוּ and וַיֵּלְכוּ are wayyiqtol forms narrating the departure of the men.
עוֹדֶנּוּ עֹמֵד: the participle with עוֹד gives a continuing state: 'still standing'.
וְאַבְרָהָם opens a clause of contrast with the wayyiqtol chain before it.
The mahpakh on וַיִּפְנוּ and the merkha on לִפְנֵי divide the verse; the silluq closes it at יְהֹוָה.
segments.note: Rashi reads the clause as a scribal correction (תִּקּוּן סוֹפְרִים): he holds that God came to Abraham and that the original text read that the LORD still stood over Abraham. The English translates the Hebrew as pointed, since the unit is translated from the witness, and records Rashi's view in the commentary.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'from there' (מִשָּׁם) means from the place where Abraham had been escorting the men. The English keeps 'from there'; the identification is recorded here.

Rashi: Abraham did not go to stand before God; God came to him and spoke, so the text should have read 'the LORD still stood over Abraham' (וַה' עוֹדֶנּוּ עוֹמֵד עַל אַבְרָהָם). He calls the present wording a scribal correction (תִּקּוּן סוֹפְרִים). The English rejects the emendation: it translates the words as they stand, and the note records Rashi's reading.

context: To 'stand before' a king or a god is the idiom for serving or petitioning him in his presence (compare Deut. 10:8; 1 Kgs 10:8). The tradition that the wording is a scribal correction (תִּקּוּן סוֹפְרִים) is rabbinic; the text as pointed has Abraham standing before the LORD.

segments.english: Abraham drew near and said, "Will you indeed sweep away a righteous person along with a wicked one?
segments.literal: and-drew-near Abraham and-said: will-also sweep-away you a-righteous with a-wicked?

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of נָגַשׁ. Rashi: this verb of approach is used for battle, for appeasement and for prayer; Abraham came with harsh words, for appeasement and for prayer.
הַ is the interrogative; אַף is 'also, even', so 'will you also / indeed sweep away'. Rashi: הֲגַם. Onkelos and Radak read אַף as 'anger'; recorded in the apparatus.
yiqtol second masculine singular, addressed to God; Ibn Ezra: transitive, 'consume'.
adjective with no senses in the lexicon.
together with: the righteous are swept together with the wicked.
adjective with no senses in the lexicon.

phrases.literal: 'will-also you-sweep-away'; Rashi: הֲגַם; the Targum and Radak read 'in anger'

phrases.english: a righteous person along with a wicked one

grammar: וַיִּגַּשׁ אַבְרָהָם וַיֹּאמַר: two wayyiqtol verbs; the approach comes first, and the speech follows it.

הַאַף: the interrogative ה (pointed with pataḥ before the guttural alef; the article would take qamets) and the adverb אַף, 'also, even': 'will you also ...?'. The Targum and Radak read אַף as 'anger'.
תִּסְפֶּה: the yiqtol is second person singular, Abraham speaking to God; the verb is transitive (Ibn Ezra) with an object left unsaid.
צַדִּיק עִם־רָשָׁע: two singular adjectives without the article, 'a righteous person with a wicked one'; the question is whether one sentence may fall on both.
segments.note: Rashi's own gloss of הַאַף is הֲגַם, 'even, also'; the Targum's 'in anger' is the reading he introduces for Onkelos. The English follows the data (אַף 'also') and keeps the anger reading in the apparatus. Ibn Ezra takes the verb as transitive, 'consume'. The quotation runs on into 18:24.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the verb וַיִּגַּשׁ is used for approach to battle, to appease, and to pray; Abraham drew near for harsh words, for appeasement and for prayer. The English keeps 'drew near' and does not name one purpose.

Rashi: הַאַף is הֲגַם, 'will you also ...'. According to the Targum of Onkelos, who rendered it with a word of anger, the meaning is 'will anger make you sweep away a righteous with a wicked?'. The English gives Rashi's own gloss and records the Targum's reading in the apparatus.
Ibn Ezra: תִּסְפֶּה is a transitive verb (פועל יוצא) with the sense 'consume', and so 'sweep away' keeps that sense.

apparatus: 18:23.4 הַאַף: Onkelos (בִּרְגַז) and Radak take אַף as 'anger', 'will you in anger sweep away?'; Rashi's own gloss is הֲגַם, 'even, also'.
context: צַדִּיק and רָשָׁע are also court words: the צַדִּיק is the one declared in the right and the רָשָׁע the one declared in the wrong (compare Deut. 25:1). Abraham's question is whether a judge may pass one sentence on both.

segments.english: Perhaps there are fifty righteous within the city. Will you indeed sweep away, and not spare Sodom for the sake of the fifty righteous who are within it?
segments.literal: perhaps there-are fifty righteous within the-city; will-also you-sweep-away and-not you-will-bear the-place for-the-sake-of fifty the-righteous who within-her

tokens.note: יֵשׁ as existence.
adjective with no senses in the lexicon.
בְּתוֹךְ: the preposition with the construct of תָּוֶךְ; no senses in the lexicon.
the interrogative ה with אַף 'also, even', as in 18:23.4.
וְלֹא: the negative joins the next verb.
נָשָׂא 'bear': Ibn Ezra reads it as 'forgive', like נושא עון (Exod. 34:7).
Ibn Ezra, the normative commentator: the place (לַמָּקוֹם) is Sodom, for whose sake Abraham drew near to save Lot. The English names Sodom.
לְמַעַן: purpose.
relative, referring back to the righteous.
בְּקִרְבָּהּ: 'within it', the city; the feminine suffix refers to the city.

phrases.literal: 'and-not you-will-bear the-place'; Ibn Ezra: the place is Sodom, and bearing here is forgiving

phrases.english: for the sake of the fifty righteous who are within it

grammar: אוּלַי introduces a tentative question: 'perhaps there are fifty'.
יֵשׁ חֲמִשִּׁים צַדִּיקִם בְּתוֹךְ הָעִיר: an existential clause with יֵשׁ; the city is where the righteous would be found.
הַאַף תִּסְפֶּה וְלֹא־תִשָּׂא: a second question, with the same verb as 18:23 and the negative on the verb of sparing.
לְמַעַן חֲמִשִּׁים הַצַּדִּיקִם אֲשֶׁר בְּקִרְבָּהּ: a purpose phrase; the relative clause 'who are within it' refers back to the righteous.
segments.note: Abraham's argument opens here and the quotation continues into 18:25, so the English has no closing quotation mark. Rashi's count is ten for each of the five cities; the English keeps the Hebrew's singular 'the city'. The English names Sodom as Ibn Ezra does, and 'spare' follows his 'forgive'.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the fifty righteous are ten for each of the five cities, since there are five places; he also asks why the righteous are destroyed if they cannot save the wicked. The English keeps 'within the city' and records Rashi's distribution.
Ibn Ezra: לֹא תִשָּׂא here is like תִּסְלַח, forgive, as in 'bearing iniquity' (נושא עון, Exod. 34:7). The English 'spare' keeps that sense: not forgive the place.
Ibn Ezra: לַמָּקוֹם is Sodom, because it was for its sake that Abraham drew near to save Lot. The English names Sodom; Radak's wider reading of the place is not adopted.
